Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

cuplyr 0.2.0

cuplyr 0.2.0 brings most of dplyr to the GPU. Nearly every dplyr verb now works on a tbl_gpu, cuplyr’s GPU table. Most run on the GPU, and the rest run in dplyr on the CPU with the same result. GPU tables are lazy by default, so an optimizer runs the whole pipeline at collect(). Also new: join_by() joins, window and rolling functions, across(), rowwise(), set operations, Parquet files on the GPU, exact integer64 columns and a conda package. cuplyr now needs RAPIDS libcudf 26.02 or later and a GPU with compute capability 7.5 or higher.

Breaking changes

  • GPU tables are lazy by default. tbl_gpu() returns a lazy table, each verb records a step, and collect(), compute() or print() run the plan. Errors in a verb’s arguments are still raised by that verb, but dplyr’s warnings, such as integer overflow or a many-to-many join, come when the plan runs, at every print() too. For eager tables, set options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager") or pass lazy = FALSE.

  • On a lazy table with pending steps, nrow() and dim() run the plan, while gpu_object_info() and gpu_memory_usage() count the rows of the table it was made from and verify_gpu_data() can return FALSE. Call compute() first.

  • cuplyr needs RAPIDS libcudf 26.02 or later and is tested on 26.10. RAPIDS 25.12 is no longer supported (#94).

  • The minimum GPU is compute capability 7.5 (Turing). The conda package and the pixi and conda install routes use a CUDA 13 build of RAPIDS, which has no code for Volta (#150).

  • Results that differed from dplyr now match it:

    • Grouping follows dplyr. summarise() drops only the last grouping column by default (.groups = "drop_last", with a message like dplyr’s), select() keeps the grouping columns, joins keep x’s groups, bind_rows() keeps the first input’s groups, collect() returns a grouped_df, and tbl_gpu() keeps the groups of a grouped_df. In 0.1.1 each of these dropped the groups. ungroup(x, col) removes only col; 0.1.1 removed every group.
    • group_by() evaluates its arguments as dplyr does. A tidyselect helper needs pick(), as in group_by(pick(all_of(cols))), and a string such as group_by("x") makes one constant group; 0.1.1 took both as column names. group_by() with no arguments removes the grouping; 0.1.1 kept it.
    • select(new = old) renames the column; 0.1.1 kept the old name.
    • summarise() aggregates follow R’s na.rm = FALSE default, so a group with an NA gives NA.
    • An ungrouped summarise() of zero rows, such as after a filter() that keeps none, returns one row, where sum() gives 0; 0.1.1 returned no rows.
    • arrange(desc(x)) puts NA last, and arrange(.by_group = TRUE) sorts the group columns ascending, as dplyr does.
    • Grouped summarise() returns groups sorted by their keys, not in hash order, and keeps rows whose key is NA as a last group; 0.1.1 dropped those rows.
    • full_join() fills the keys of rows found only in y; 0.1.1 left them NA.
    • Integer +, - and * return integers, not doubles. An overflow gives NA with R’s warning.
    • In summarise(), sum() of integers or logicals, such as sum(x > 0), and an ungrouped n() return integers, not doubles, and min() and max() of a logical column return integers, not logicals. A sum() too large for an integer is a double, as in R.
    • NaN stays NaN; it used to become NA on upload.
    • integer64 columns are exact and collect to bit64::integer64; they used to be uploaded as doubles, which corrupted them.
    • POSIXct columns keep their time zone instead of coming back in UTC.
    • A GPU table made from a data.frame collects to a data.frame, with its attributes.
    • Factor columns stay factors after select(), joins, bind_rows(), bind_cols(), a lazy mutate() and as summarise() group keys, and ordered factors stay ordered; 0.1.1 returned integer codes, or plain factors. Joins match factor keys by their labels; 0.1.1 matched the codes, which paired the wrong rows when the two tables’ levels differed.

  • Uploading a column with no GPU type (difftime, hms, ts, POSIXlt, a list, a matrix with several columns, …) raises an error that names the column, instead of losing its class. So does a verb that makes a difftime on the CPU, such as end - start on dates. Returning such columns is an open issue (#65).

  • print() uses a tibble-style # A tbl_gpu: n x m header, R type labels and factor labels.

  • show_query() is now a method for dplyr’s generic. Its argument is x, and it prints the plan as R code and returns x invisibly.

  • $, [[ and length() of a GPU table give its columns, as for a data frame, and names<- accepts NA and empty names. In 0.1.1, $, [[ and length() gave the object’s internal fields, such as x$schema and x$ptr, and names<- refused those names (#4). split(), with(), subset(), t(), as.environment(), is.na() and anyNA() of a GPU table raise an error; they used to act on the internal fields.

Installation and requirements

  • cuplyr is available as a conda package, r-cuplyr, on the bbtheo channel on anaconda.org. It is a binary for RAPIDS 26.10 and CUDA 13 that needs an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 13 but no CUDA toolkit or compiler. Install it with conda, mamba or pixi; the README has the commands (#135).

  • install.sh and install_cuplyr() build cuplyr against libcudf from pixi, conda or the system (--method= picks one). The conda route installs RAPIDS 26.10 for CUDA 13 with the CUDA compiler, and the pixi environments carry the CUDA 13 build tools, so neither needs a system toolkit (#157).

  • ./configure stops with a clear message when libcudf is older than 26.02, and prefers the CUDA toolkit of a conda or pixi environment (#38, #94).

  • New check_deps() checks the driver, CUDA toolkit, libcudf and R packages, verify_installation() runs a small GPU round trip, and diagnostics() reports versions, the GPU, the memory resource and every option for a bug report, as text or JSON. diagnose_loader() shows how cuplyr’s shared library resolves libstdc++, libcudf and libcuda (#14, #49).

New features

Verbs

  • Anything with no GPU form runs in dplyr on the CPU instead of failing. options(cuplyr.fallback = "warn") reports each fallback with its reason and the data moved; "error" forbids them.

  • Newly on the GPU: filter_out(), transmute(), rename(), rename_with(), relocate(), distinct(), pull(), count(), tally(), add_count(), add_tally(), reframe(), the slice() family, top_n(), sample_n(), group_split(), group_trim(), group_data() and the other grouping functions, rowwise(), the rows_*() verbs and the _at(), _all() and _if() verbs.

  • group_map(), group_modify(), group_nest(), nest_by(), nest_join() and do() run on the CPU.

  • .by works in mutate(), filter(), summarise(), reframe() and the slice() family, and grouped verbs run per group on the GPU. group_by() takes computed keys and .drop = FALSE.

  • rowwise() runs elementwise expressions and row aggregates such as sum(c_across(a:e)) on the GPU. On 1e5 rows that takes milliseconds, where dplyr takes about twenty seconds.

  • [, [<- for whole columns, as.data.frame(), as_tibble(), glimpse(), head(), rbind(), cbind(), vctrs::vec_slice(), vctrs::vec_size(), dplyr::bind_rows() and purrr::map_dfr() work on GPU tables.

Lazy plans

  • The optimizer now also prunes unused columns below summarise(), arrange() and other barriers.

  • explain() and show_query() print the plan as R code without running it, including the columns a Parquet scan reads and the reason for each CPU fallback (#10).

  • Printing a lazy table runs the whole plan to show the first rows and keeps nothing; a plan over a Parquet file prints its schema unless it only selects or renames columns.

  • A step whose result type or error depends on the data (an integer sum(), a join with unmatched = "error") runs at the verb, as in eager mode; options(cuplyr.plan_break = "warn") reports it.

Expressions

  • filter(), mutate() and summarise() share one expression engine that runs on the GPU:

    • arithmetic, comparisons, logic, %in%, is.na(), is.nan(), between(), near() and math functions, round() with R’s rule;
    • if_else(), case_when(), case_match(), coalesce(), na_if(), recode() and dplyr 1.2’s recode_values(), replace_values(), replace_when(), when_any() and when_all();
    • window functions: lag(), lead(), the ranking and cumulative functions, consecutive_id(), first(), last(), nth(), order_by() and grouped aggregates such as x - mean(x);
    • summaries: median(), quantile(), n_distinct(), any(), all() and the rest, of any expression and with arithmetic around them (#22);
    • base string functions: paste(), substr(), nchar(), toupper(), trimws(), grepl(), sub(), gsub(), startsWith(), …;
    • factor comparisons with labels and as.character();
    • Date and POSIXct literals, casts and date + n, lubridate’s date parts (year(), hour(), wday(), …) and fixed-unit floor_date(), ceiling_date() and round_date().

  • across(), if_any(), if_all(), cur_group_id() and cur_column() run on the GPU; pick() as a data frame and cur_group() run on the CPU.

  • A function of your own named like one cuplyr runs on the GPU (mean(), lag(), …) is the one called, as in dplyr.

Joins and set operations

  • The mutating joins, semi_join(), anti_join() and cross_join() run on the GPU, with join_by() equality, inequality, between(), within(), overlaps() and closest() conditions. multiple, unmatched, relationship, na_matches, keep and suffix follow dplyr, and keys of different types combine by vctrs’ rules, an all-NA key included (#70).

  • union(), union_all(), intersect(), setdiff(), symdiff() and setequal() run on the GPU. bind_rows() follows vctrs’ type rules and binds factors to the union of their levels. Binds and set operations return a lazy table when any input is lazy (#20, #70).

Parquet

  • New read_parquet_gpu() and write_parquet_gpu() read and write Parquet files on the GPU; only compressed bytes cross the PCIe bus.

  • A lazy read reads only the columns the plan uses and skips row groups for simple filters on integer, integer64, Date and POSIXct columns. options(cuplyr.parquet_pushdown = FALSE) turns this off; use it for untrusted files, as malformed statistics can crash the session.

Types

  • integer64 comparisons, sorting, grouping, joins and binds run exactly on the GPU; arithmetic and aggregates follow bit64 on the CPU.

  • NaN counts as missing in is.na(), comparisons, arrange() and the na.rm = TRUE reducers, as in R.

  • An infinite or out-of-range Date or POSIXct value warns on upload and becomes NA; it used to give NA or a wrong date silently.

  • Columns keep their element names, attributes and one-column matrix shape by dplyr’s rules, and tables with rows but no columns work (#19, #21, #56).

  • Strings go to the GPU as UTF-8, and columns with more than 2 GiB of characters work.

Rolling windows

  • New roll_mean(), roll_sum(), roll_min(), roll_max() and roll_sd() run on the GPU in mutate() and filter(), grouped or not, in time that doesn’t depend on the window width. data.table::frollmean() and its siblings work as aliases. New roll_median() matches stats::median() exactly and runs on the CPU.

Options, errors and memory

  • New cuplyr_options() lists every option with its value and where it came from; ?"cuplyr-options" documents them. An invalid value warns once, with class cuplyr_warning_invalid_option, and the default is used.

  • Errors and warnings have dplyr’s class, message and call for missing columns, calls dplyr rejects and the min() and max() warnings for empty groups. Errors in mutate() carry dplyr’s class and its In argument: context (#13, #20, #24, #28, #30, #69).

  • cuplyr installs CUDA’s stream-ordered ("async") memory resource when it loads. It reserves a quarter of the free GPU memory, at most 1 GiB, and keeps the memory of freed tables for reuse, so other processes see it as used until gpu_gc() returns it to the device and reports it in released_bytes. Each call frees its temporary GPU tables when it returns. Before loading, set options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "pool") for RMM’s pool, cuplyr.pool_initial to reserve less, or cuplyr.release_threshold to release memory automatically (vignette("memory")).

  • gpu_memory_state() reports the memory resource, pool_bytes and pool_used_bytes. used_bytes counts the memory the resource holds, so it no longer falls when a table is freed, and the freed_bytes of gpu_gc() counts memory freed inside the resource.

  • New gpu_sync() waits for queued GPU work, for timing. A step that runs out of GPU memory is retried once after garbage collection, and the final error says what helps (#13).

  • Loading cuplyr sets the environment variable LIBCUDF_USE_DEBUG_STREAM_POOL unless it is set, so that Parquet reads don’t slow later verbs (?read_parquet_gpu).

  • New vignette("performance") and vignette("memory"), and vignette("query-optimization") matches the optimizer. Help-page examples run (#39).

Performance

  • Recording a mutate() on a lazy table no longer slows down as the plan grows, and a column passed through a verb is shared instead of copied.

  • Each filter() or mutate() call runs as one fused GPU kernel where it can, and computes a repeated round(), %in% or string call once (#17).

  • A lazy arrange(x) |> head(n) on one numeric or date key, and slice_min()/slice_max() (grouped too), use a top-k selection instead of a full sort.

Minor improvements and bug fixes

  • right_join() works (it failed on every call) and returns dplyr’s row order and keys.

  • summarise() accepts dplyr::n() and stats::sd(), names an unnamed expression after its text, and works lazily with sd() and var().

  • Lazy plans with chained joins, or a mutate() that overwrites a column, give the right result.

  • The namespace loads with only its stated dependencies (it failed when utils was not attached, which R CMD check reports), rowwise()’s method takes data like the generic, and the C++ code no longer uses the APIs libcudf 26.10 deprecates (#166).

  • ?tbl_gpu explains what a GPU table is and how to work with one: lazy by default, collect(), compute(), explain(), eager mode and the column types. The verbs’ help pages say what runs on the GPU, what runs in dplyr on the CPU and where the result differs from dplyr, without internal development notes (#159).

cuplyr 0.1.1

Bug fixes

  • collect() now correctly restores factor columns with their original levels. Previously, factor columns were returned as integer codes instead of factors (#3).

  • names<-() now validates the replacement value before assignment. It errors if the new names have wrong length, contain NA values, empty strings, or are not character (#4).

Build system

  • Fixed CCCL (CUDA Core Compute Libraries) header detection for RAPIDS 25.12+ in pixi/conda environments where headers are located in a rapids/ subdirectory. The configure script now automatically detects <cuda/stream_ref> and related headers.

  • Reordered include paths so CUDF/RMM headers take precedence over system CUDA headers, ensuring consistent CCCL versions.

Documentation

  • Added pkgdown documentation site with vignettes for getting started, complex analysis workflows, and query optimization.

cuplyr 0.1.0

Lazy evaluation

  • tbl_gpu() gains a lazy argument to enable deferred execution. Operations build an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) that is optimized and executed only when collect() or compute() is called. Set globally with options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "lazy") or CUPLYR_EXEC_MODE=lazy environment variable.

  • Added an AST optimizer that applies multiple optimization passes before execution:

    • Projection pruning: push column selection close to data sources
    • Mutate fusion: combine consecutive mutate operations
    • Dead column pruning: remove unused intermediate columns
    • Filter pushdown: move filters earlier in the pipeline, including across joins
    • Filter reordering: execute cheaper filters first
    • Filter fusion: combine multiple filters into single GPU kernel

  • compute() executes pending lazy operations and keeps the result on GPU.

  • collapse() inserts an optimization barrier without executing.

  • as_lazy() and as_eager() switch execution modes mid-pipeline.

  • is_lazy() and has_pending_ops() check the current execution state.

  • show_query() displays the pending operation tree for debugging.

Join operations

  • Added inner_join(), left_join(), right_join(), and full_join() for combining GPU tables (#2). Joins support automatic key detection (natural join), named vectors in by for different key names, suffix for column name conflicts, keep for retaining join keys, and copy to auto-transfer data frames to GPU.

Bind operations

  • Added bind_rows() for vertically combining GPU tables with automatic schema unification and type promotion.

  • Added bind_cols() for horizontally combining GPU tables with .name_repair for duplicate column handling.

  • Both bind functions automatically materialize lazy tables before binding.

cuplyr 0.0.1

Initial release of cuplyr, a GPU-accelerated dplyr backend using NVIDIA’s libcudf library.

Core functionality

  • tbl_gpu() transfers R data frames to GPU memory, returning a tbl_gpu object that works with dplyr verbs.

  • collect() transfers GPU data back to R as a tibble.

  • as_tbl_gpu() coerces data frames to GPU tables.

  • is_tbl_gpu() tests if an object is a GPU table.

dplyr verbs

  • filter() supports scalar comparisons (x > 5, x == "a") and column-to-column comparisons (x > y). Supports boolean vectors as filter masks.

  • select() supports column selection by name, position, and tidyselect helpers.

  • mutate() supports arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /, ^) with scalars and between columns. Supports left-associative chains (e.g., a + b + c).

  • arrange() sorts by one or more columns with desc() support for descending order. Supports .by_group = TRUE for grouped tables.

  • group_by() sets grouping metadata for subsequent aggregation. ungroup() removes grouping.

  • summarise() computes grouped aggregations with support for sum(), mean(), min(), max(), n(), sd(), and var(). Supports expressions inside aggregation functions (e.g., sum(x > 0)).

Type support

  • Supported R types: numeric (FLOAT64), integer (INT32), character (STRING), logical (BOOL8), Date (TIMESTAMP_DAYS), and POSIXct (TIMESTAMP_MICROSECONDS).

  • factor columns are converted to INT32 codes.

  • integer64 columns are converted to FLOAT64 with a warning about precision loss for values exceeding 2^53.

GPU memory utilities

  • gpu_memory_usage() estimates GPU memory footprint of a tbl_gpu object.

  • gpu_memory_state() returns current GPU memory usage (total, free, used).

  • gpu_gc() forces garbage collection to free GPU memory from unreferenced tables.

  • gpu_object_info() returns detailed information about a GPU table.

  • verify_gpu_data() confirms data resides on GPU, not in R memory.

  • gpu_size_comparison() compares R object size vs GPU data size.

GPU information

  • has_gpu() checks if a compatible GPU is available.

  • gpu_details() returns GPU device information (name, compute capability, memory).
